events.title: EDSAC runs its first programs
events.summary: On May 6, 1949, the EDSAC at Cambridge ran its first programs — including a table of squares written by Beatrice Worsley.
events.about: EDSAC was among the first practical stored-program computers, keeping both instructions and data in memory. That May day proved Maurice Wilkes's design worked end to end. Wheeler's Initial Orders — a built-in program that translated mnemonic instructions from paper tape — were already in place and would soon be recognized as the first assembler.

narrative.whyChosen: EDSAC's first successful run marked stored-program computing working outside a lab prototype.
narrative.whyImportant: It showed that programs and data could live in the same memory — the model every modern computer uses.
narrative.problemSolved: Earlier machines like ENIAC were reprogrammed by rewiring; EDSAC loaded new tasks from tape into memory.

sources.title: Computing History — EDSAC runs its first program (May 6, 1949)

events.title: Wheeler's EDSAC Initial Orders add the first assembler
events.summary: By May 1949, David Wheeler's Initial Orders let EDSAC translate mnemonic instructions from paper tape into machine code — the first assembler.
events.about: Before assemblers, programmers punched raw binary numbers for every instruction. Wheeler's Initial Orders — a small boot program loaded at startup — read labels like `A 80` from tape and wrote the 17-bit words EDSAC executed. The same month EDSAC ran its first user programs, this loader made programming faster and launched the idea behind every compiler since.

narrative.whyChosen: Initial Orders turned mnemonic programming into machine code automatically — the birth of assembly language.
narrative.whyImportant: Automating instruction translation made programming repeatable and scalable as computers grew more capable.
narrative.problemSolved: Human transcription of machine instructions was slow, error-prone, and did not scale.

sources.title: Royal Society — Wheeler, Programme organization and initial orders for the EDSAC (1950)
